title: Orchard School District Parcel Tax
summary: Measure R creates a new parcel tax in Orchard School District, a small single-school district in North San Jose, charged at 4 cents per building square foot (capped at $89 for residential parcels and $7,500 for non-residential parcels) for 8 years starting July 1, 2027, raising an estimated $1.4 million a year for STEAM education, visual and performing arts, and teacher recruitment and retention. It requires two-thirds voter approval and, unlike Cambrian School District's Measure Q on the same ballot, does not stack on top of any existing parcel tax; it does arrive less than two years after voters approved the district's $30 million Measure GG facilities bond in November 2024.
what_it_really_means: The official ballot question reads: 'To enhance and create quality educational opportunities, attract and retain teachers and staff, support Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts and Mathematics (STEAM) education and visual and performing arts, shall the Orchard School District measure levying a parcel tax at the rate of 4 cents per building square foot (not-to-exceed $7,500 non-residential and $89 residential per parcel), raising $1.4 million annually for eight years beginning July 1, 2027, with senior exemptions and all expenditures audited be adopted?' per the county Registrar's local-measures list. This is materially different from most Santa Clara County school parcel taxes, including Cambrian School District's Measure Q on this same ballot, which charge a flat dollar amount per parcel regardless of building size. Measure R instead scales with the square footage of the building on the parcel, up to a cap.

Working the math the ballot text implies: a typical single-family home of roughly 1,800 square feet would owe about $72 a year (1,800 x $0.04); the $89 residential cap is reached at 2,225 square feet, so any home at or above that size pays the same flat $89 as a home exactly at 2,225 square feet. On the non-residential side, the $7,500 cap is reached at 187,500 square feet of building area; a small retail or office building well under that size pays the full 4 cents per square foot (a 10,000-square-foot building would owe $400), while a very large single building, such as a large office or industrial campus, pays no more than $7,500 regardless of how far past 187,500 square feet it goes. That structure means the effective per-square-foot rate falls as a non-residential building grows past the cap threshold, a form of regressivity within the non-residential tier that the ballot question's headline rate does not surface. Orchard School District's boundaries are reported to cover part of the North San Jose commercial corridor near West Tasman Drive, in the vicinity of Cisco Systems' San Jose campus, based on a web search summary; this analysis could not directly confirm from a district boundary map or the Registrar's filings whether any specific large commercial campus falls inside the district and would be affected by the non-residential cap, so that point should be read as unconfirmed context rather than a verified fact.

Neither the county's Impartial Analysis PDF nor the district's full ballot-measure text (Notice of Election) PDF could be read for this analysis: both are hosted behind Cloudflare bot protection that returned HTTP 403 to both a direct fetch and an r.jina.ai proxy fetch, and no archived copy was found on the Wayback Machine. As a result, this analysis could not confirm one operationally important detail the ballot question does not answer: whether a parcel's 'building square foot' figure for tax purposes comes from county assessor/building-permit records (independently verifiable) or is self-reported by the property owner (harder to audit or enforce). No source reached for this analysis, including the district's own website, states which method applies. This is a genuine gap, not a settled fact being omitted; a voter cannot tell from the ballot question, the district's public pages, or (because they could not be read) the county's own analysis documents, how the square-footage figure will be determined or challenged.

Orchard School District does not appear to have any existing parcel tax that Measure R would stack on top of. Searches of the district's own site and general web search turned up no parcel tax measure predating Measure R; the district's most recent prior ballot measure is Measure GG, a $30 million school facilities general obligation bond approved by voters in November 2024 at a rate of $12 per $100,000 of assessed value. A GO bond is a fundamentally different instrument from a parcel tax: it is repaid through an ad valorem property tax line tied to a property's assessed value, not a flat or square-footage-based per-parcel charge, and California law (Education Code Section 15278) requires a bond to have an independent citizens' bond oversight committee, which the district's website references via a 'Bond Oversight Committee' navigation link (the linked page itself returned a 404 when checked). So while Measure R does not stack on a prior parcel tax the way Cambrian's Measure Q stacks on Cambrian's Measure A, a property owner in Orchard School District who already pays the Measure GG bond levy would, if Measure R passes, be paying two separate new education-related charges on the same property tax bill within about a three-year span, a combination the Measure R ballot question does not mention.

The spending categories are broadly defined and not tied to a binding formula. The ballot question lists STEAM education and visual/performing arts alongside the more general goals of 'quality educational opportunities' and teacher/staff recruitment and retention; a search-summarized version of the district's own materials also lists core academics (math, science, reading, technology), literacy skills, student mental health support, and technology/lab resources as intended uses, categories broader than the 'STEAM/arts' framing suggests and not all traceable to the ballot text itself. No source reached for this analysis, including the inaccessible Impartial Analysis, describes a dollar-by-category spending plan; the district's Board of Trustees would retain year-to-year discretion over how the roughly $1.4 million raised is allocated across these purposes.

Accountability is described, per search-summarized district materials, as deposit into a separate dedicated account, annual expenditure reporting, and an annual independent financial audit, on top of the statutory floor that all California parcel taxes must meet (Government Code Section 50075.1, an annual report to the governing board). No source reached for this analysis describes an independent citizens' oversight committee specific to Measure R; that is a different, and generally weaker, accountability structure than the citizens' bond oversight committee state law mandates for the district's separate Measure GG bond.

No argument against Measure R was filed with the Registrar of Voters, so the official ballot pamphlet will carry only the argument in favor; that argument's full text could not be read for this analysis for the same Cloudflare-blocking reason as the Impartial Analysis. The Silicon Valley Taxpayers Association, in its 2026 general-election voter guide, separately and publicly lists 'Measure R - Orchard School District $1,400,000 parcel tax for 8 years. (2/3 vote)' among the local tax measures it recommends Santa Clara County voters reject, so organized opposition exists even though none was formally filed in the pamphlet.

The Orchard School District Board of Trustees approved placing the measure on the November 3, 2026 ballot at its July 29, 2026 meeting, per the district's own announcement. A separate board-meeting index found by search references a 'Resolution #061626-1: RESOLUTION OF THE GOVERNING BOARD OF THE ORCHARD SCHOOL DISTRICT CALLING A GENERAL ELECTION TO BE HELD ON TUESDAY, NOVEMBER 03, 2026'; this analysis could not directly open that board-agenda system to confirm the resolution's adoption date, its exact relationship to the July 29 announcement, or the roll-call vote count, so those details rest on a search-engine summary rather than a directly read primary document.

fiscal_impact.state_cost: none. The measure does not obligate state funds.
fiscal_impact.local_cost: none to other local government bodies. The cost falls on owners of taxable parcels within Orchard School District: a new parcel tax of 4 cents per building square foot per year, capped at $89 for residential parcels and $7,500 for non-residential parcels, for 8 years, with exemptions for seniors and, per search-summarized district materials, recipients of SSI or SSDI. This is a new charge; Orchard School District does not appear to have a pre-existing parcel tax for it to replace or add to, though the district's separate Measure GG general obligation bond (approved November 2024, $30 million, $12 per $100,000 assessed value) continues to be levied independently.
fiscal_impact.revenue_change: A new annual revenue stream for the district of approximately $1.4 million, with no prior parcel-tax revenue to compare it against.
fiscal_impact.ongoing_vs_one_time: Recurring annual levy for 8 years if approved, beginning with the 2027-28 fiscal year (July 1, 2027) per the ballot question. The ballot question does not mention an inflation adjustment or a 'continuance subject to voter approval' clause of the kind Cambrian's Measure Q includes, so on current sources this appears to be a flat, non-escalating rate for the full 8-year term, though this analysis could not confirm that against the unreadable full ballot text.
fiscal_impact.narrative: Measure R would raise roughly $11.2 million over its 8-year term at the stated $1.4 million-a-year rate, a cumulative figure the ballot question's per-year number does not surface. Because it is a parcel tax funding programs and staffing rather than facilities, it carries no borrowing or interest cost, unlike the district's separate Measure GG bond. The two measures are financially distinct instruments (a per-square-foot parcel tax versus an assessed-value-based bond levy) but land on the same property tax bill within about three years of each other, so the fiscal picture for an Orchard-area property owner includes both even though Measure R's ballot question addresses only itself.

new_taxes: A new parcel tax in Orchard School District at 4 cents per building square foot per year, capped at $89 for residential parcels and $7,500 for non-residential parcels, for 8 years starting July 1, 2027, with senior and (per search-summarized district materials) SSI/SSDI exemptions, raising an estimated $1.4 million per year.

new_spending_areas: STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts and Mathematics) education.
Teacher and staff recruitment and retention.
Core academic programs, literacy skills, student mental health support, and technology/lab resources (per search-summarized district materials, not stated in the ballot question itself).
spending.funding_source: A new parcel tax based on building square footage (4 cents per square foot, capped at $89 residential / $7,500 non-residential per parcel per year), deposited, per search-summarized district materials, into a separate dedicated account; not a bond, so it carries no borrowing or interest cost.

control_and_power: The Orchard School District Board of Trustees placed Measure R on the ballot, approving it at the board's July 29, 2026 meeting per the district's own announcement; a separately indexed board resolution, titled 'RESOLUTION OF THE GOVERNING BOARD OF THE ORCHARD SCHOOL DISTRICT CALLING A GENERAL ELECTION TO BE HELD ON TUESDAY, NOVEMBER 03, 2026' and referenced as Resolution #061626-1 in a board-meeting index found by search, could not be directly read to confirm its adoption date or vote count. The measure itself then requires a two-thirds vote of the electorate. Once approved, the five-member Board of Trustees (Virginia Varela-Campos, president; Renee Lo, vice president; Jeff Tang, clerk; Karl Jacobson; and Katherine Kasolas-Jacobson, per the district's board-members page), together with Superintendent Dr. Jeffrey Bowman's administration, would decide each year how the roughly $1.4 million raised is allocated across the measure's broadly stated purposes, subject to a dedicated account, annual expenditure reporting, and an annual independent audit described in search-summarized district materials, plus the statutory floor requiring an annual report to the board (Government Code Section 50075.1). No source reached for this analysis describes an independent citizens' oversight committee specific to Measure R, a lighter accountability structure than the citizens' bond oversight committee state law requires for the district's separate Measure GG facilities bond.
loopholes: Whether the 'building square foot' figure used to compute the tax comes from county assessor/building-permit records or is self-reported by the property owner is not stated in any source this analysis could read; the two PDFs that would likely answer this (the Impartial Analysis and the district's full ballot-measure text) were both blocked by Cloudflare bot protection on every fetch attempted, including an r.jina.ai proxy. This matters directly for enforcement: a self-reported figure is far easier to underreport than an assessor-verified one.

The non-residential $7,500 cap is reached at 187,500 square feet, so very large single buildings pay a lower effective per-square-foot rate than mid-size commercial buildings under that threshold; a small business well under the cap pays the full 4 cents per square foot on every square foot, while a large single-tenant building far past the cap pays a flat $7,500 regardless of additional size.

There is no binding, itemized spending plan tying specific dollar shares of the roughly $1.4 million annual revenue to any of the listed purposes (STEAM, arts, teacher retention, and, per search-summarized materials, mental health and other categories); the Board of Trustees retains broad year-to-year discretion within those categories.

The accountability mechanism described in search-summarized district materials is a dedicated account, annual reporting, and an annual audit, not an independent citizens' oversight committee; no source found for this analysis confirmed or ruled out such a committee for Measure R specifically.

No opposing argument was filed with the Registrar of Voters, so the official ballot pamphlet will contain only the case in favor, even though the Silicon Valley Taxpayers Association has publicly recommended a NO vote.
unexpected_provisions: The per-square-foot mechanism is unusual: most Santa Clara County school parcel taxes, including Cambrian School District's Measure Q on this same ballot, charge a flat dollar amount per parcel rather than scaling with building size.

The ballot question's 'STEAM/arts' framing does not disclose that, per search-summarized district materials, the intended uses also include core academics, literacy, student mental health support, and technology/lab resources, categories broader than STEAM and the arts.

The ballot question does not mention that the district's voters approved a separate $30 million facilities bond, Measure GG, in November 2024, whose ad valorem levy continues independently of Measure R and would land on the same property tax bill.

Exemptions for seniors and, per search-summarized district materials, SSI/SSDI recipients exist, but this analysis found no stated application deadline or process for either, unlike some other Santa Clara County parcel tax exemptions that specify a firm annual deadline.
pros: Measure R funds STEAM education, visual and performing arts, and teacher recruitment and retention, areas supporters argue are chronically underfunded by state per-pupil funding alone.

The tax is described, per search-summarized district materials, as scaling with building size and capped on both ends, which supporters can frame as more proportionate than a flat per-parcel charge that treats a small condo the same as a large home or business.
Funds would go into a dedicated account with annual expenditure reporting and an annual independent audit, on top of the statutory minimum annual report all California parcel taxes require.
Exemptions exist for seniors and, per search-summarized district materials, recipients of SSI or SSDI.

No formal opposition argument was filed with the county, indicating limited organized local opposition to the specific measure text, even though the Silicon Valley Taxpayers Association opposes it on general tax-policy grounds.

Unlike some neighboring districts on this same ballot, Orchard School District does not have a pre-existing parcel tax, so Measure R is not layering a new charge onto an already-stacked parcel-tax burden.
cons: The Silicon Valley Taxpayers Association recommends a NO vote on Measure R as part of its broader opposition to new local tax measures on the November 2026 Santa Clara County ballot.

Whether the square-footage figure used to calculate each parcel's tax is verified against county assessor records or simply self-reported could not be confirmed from any source reached for this analysis, because the two primary documents that would likely answer it were inaccessible; that is a real, unresolved enforcement question, not a settled reassurance.

The non-residential cap structure means a very large single building pays a lower effective per-square-foot rate than a mid-size commercial building under the $7,500 cap threshold (187,500 square feet), a form of regressivity the ballot question's headline rate does not surface.

Measure R arrives less than two years after voters approved the district's $30 million Measure GG facilities bond (November 2024), adding a second new education-related charge to the same property tax bill within a short span, context the ballot question does not disclose.
The measure requires a two-thirds supermajority to pass, a high bar that lets a well-organized minority block it even if a simple majority of voters support it.

Neither the county's Impartial Analysis nor the Primary Argument In-Favor, nor the district's full ballot-measure text, could be read in full for this research; all three PDFs returned Cloudflare 403 errors on every access method attempted, limiting independent verification of the county's own official analysis and the measure's complete legal text.

The Board of Trustees retains broad, unitemized discretion over how the roughly $1.4 million raised annually is allocated across the measure's several stated purposes, with no binding spending formula found in sources reached for this analysis.
